newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa tightens border regulations to cut crime.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa tightens border regulations to cut crime.

text.p: South Africa is seeking to cut border control losses estimated as high as 17 billion rand ($3.8 billion) a year by shutting two-thirds of its border posts for bulk commercial traffic, government officials said on Wednesday.

The cabinet on Wednesday adopted recommendations to reduce the number of border posts open to bulk commercial traffic to 34 points from 95 and unify previously fragmented border controls to embrace immigration, customs and border police.

"For those bringing in goods illegally, there's been a veritable picnic over the last few years," the Secretary for Safety and Security, Azhar Cachalia, told a news conference after the cabinet meeting.
"In our view this represents a major and very concrete step forward in the fight against crime," he said.

Stricter controls will be enforced at the border posts, which will remain open to commercial traffic. Changes at land border posts are expected to take three months to implement and to be completed at the major airports within six months.
Cachalia said cross border flights landing at unauthorised airports will be seized and the Air Force will be used to track illegal flights.
Customs procedures are also being upgraded with advice from the British and the United States governments. Normal tourist traffic will not be affected.
Cachalia said past infringements included smuggling, which had led to loss of revenues running into billions of rand and which undermined industrial and trade policy.
Other problems were fraudulent exports, which had resulted in evasion of Value Added Tax and syndicate crimes, including gun-running and illegal drug imports.
"The loss to the government from border control problems has been estimated by some to be as high as 17 billion rand a year, although accurate figures are difficult to come by," he said.
Police Senior Superintendent Brian van Niekerk told the conference the new measures were expected to halve the number of vehicles ferried across the borders illegally within three months.
